pr_body:
OpenGL uses the diamond exit rule to rasterize lines. If we don't shift
the points down and to the right by 0.5, the line can sometimes miss a
pixel when it shouldn't. The final fragment of a line isn't drawn. By
drawing the lines clockwise, we can avoid a missing pixel in the rectangle.
See section 3.4.1 in the OpenGL 1.5 specification.
Fixes #32279
pr_comments: Changes look good. Can you check that the spec is the same for 2.1 and 3.3?

The idea of diamond exit is explained here: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/direct3d11/d3d10-graphics-programming-guide-rasterizer-stage-rules. (This is for directx, but it should be the same in OpenGL.)To make sure that the first pixel of a line is drawn, it should start at the x in the center(0.5, 0.5) of the pixel area. If we start to draw at the top left(0,0), the line might never cut the diamond pattern of the first pixel, leaving a gap at the corner. This works fine on my nvidia GPU, but on my integrated intel haswell gpu it doesn't(At least the missing pixel is now consistently at the top right). I don't think it's possible to create cross platform pixel perfect lines with OpenGL. The algorithm is in the specification for OpenGL 2.1 and 3.3, but vendors are allowed to use slightly different algorithms. It might be interesting if someone with a AMD GPU or more modern intel GPU could test this.
More resources here, explained pretty succinctly. http://graphics-software-engineer.blogspot.com/2012/04/rasterization-rules.html

> I think it'd be good to write a comment to explain why `0.5` is being added to the values 

Changes seem good to me, but I agree that adding a short comment in both GLES2 and GLES3 before the `verts` definition would be good to make things explicit.

It this change causing this issue?

Fills my control fully - all good
```
func _draw():
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2(), Vector2(32,32)), Color.red, true)
```
But drawing only the outline has an offset
```
func _draw():
	draw_rect(Rect2(Vector2(), Vector2(32,32)), Color.red, false)
```
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4741886/68066157-9e269980-fd33-11e9-831c-aadf127372fa.png)
Can't reproduce with your code. Would be helpful if you could add a minimal reproduction project.
Can you try to scale the Control by 16,16 this is what I do in my case

I understand why this was added, but this is not the right way and it will likely need to be reverted. The reason is that lines can be used with a canvas scale and this will break them.

Researching a better solution is probably a better idea, or likely attempting to implement it in 4.0, which supplies the separate canvas matrices.
I suggest doing the pixel shifting at matrix level instead for lines.
Pushing a partial revert of the line shifting in #33427, as @reduz mentioned that the clockwise draw in CanvasItem is otherwise fine.

issue_context.title: Missing pixel when using draw_rect
issue_context.body:
**Godot version:**
3.2-dev (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/5ffae0d299aa799c7787e01f3cfe5e377b78a411)

**OS/device including version:**
Windows 10 64-bit

**Issue description:**
A small issue, but an issue nevertheless. When drawing with the `draw_rect` function, there is a missing pixel in the lower left corner. If using fill, the bug doesn't introduce itself. This happens on both GLES3 and GLES2.

![missing_pixel](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/359786/65432751-6f5c0000-de24-11e9-9105-b997f64bdd6a.png)


**Steps to reproduce:**
Just put this script to a Node2D: 
```
extends Node2D

func _draw():
	draw_rect(Rect2(1, 1, 100, 100), Color(0.5, 0.8, 0.5), false)
```

**Minimal reproduction project:**
[DrawRectBug.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/3642497/DrawRectBug.zip)
comments: Is it always missing if you draw that rectangle at different positions, and with decimal coordinates?

I can reproduce this on commit https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/a226d63f6815836284f947ccc56b688448381f84. Note that the missing pixel won't always be in the bottom-left corner; it depends on the rectangle's position (see the demo project below).

**Demo project:** [DrawRectBug_with_anim.zip](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/files/3642727/DrawRectBug_with_anim.zip)

This bug can be reproduced on both GLES3 and GLES2 renderers. Changing the stretch mode to `2d` or `disabled` doesn't solve the issue either.

~~A half pixel offset is required to make this work: `draw_rect(Rect2(0.5, 0.5, 100, 100), Color(0.5, 0.8, 0.5), false)`
(though, pixel snap has to be disabled)~~
Edit: actually that's not quite correct either.

Note that this only applies to unfilled rectangles, as mentioned in the original post.

> Is it always missing if you draw that rectangle at different positions, and with decimal coordinates?

If I'm using integer coordinates, then it's always in the bottom left corner. If I'm using decimal coordinates, then it shifts between the bottom left and bottom right corner.

![itsaproblem](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/359786/65439690-3fb2f500-de30-11e9-8991-33d851e536b4.gif)

Tested with this script (and tried changing the `increment` to `0.5`, when testing the decimal coordinates):
```
extends Node2D

var pos_x := 0.0
var pos_y := 0.0
var increment := 1

func _draw():
	draw_rect(Rect2(pos_x, pos_y, 100, 100), Color(0.5, 0.8, 0.5), false)

func _process(delta):
	if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_up"):
		pos_y -= increment
	elif Input.is_action_pressed("ui_down"):
		pos_y += increment
		
	if Input.is_action_pressed("ui_left"):
		pos_x -= increment
	elif Input.is_action_pressed("ui_right"):
		pos_x += increment
		
	update()
```

Anti-aliased version, GLES3:

`draw_rect(Rect2(1, 1, 100, 100), Color(0.5, 0.8, 0.5), false, 1.0, true)`

![antialiased-rect](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/17108460/65445020-f5367600-de39-11e9-8283-505731e2d804.png)
For the record, the `draw_rect()` `width` and `antialiased` parameters were added in #30461.

review_comments:
The order used to be "add `Point2` then add `Size2`, but now it's no longer consistent, you have `Point2`/`Size2` here, but `Size2`/`Point2` for the next two calls.
It's the same typedef so it doesn't matter so much, but the inconsistency looks weird.
Yes. Size2 for all probably makes more sense semantically.
